issues.issue: The clause authorises payment "to any other person for the use and benefit of a minor" with a full discharge to the Trustee, an open-ended catch-all beside the specific alternatives of guardian or the minor himself. Who qualifies as such an "other person" is left without any standard.

Permitting outright payment to or for a minor conflicts with Article VI(4), which directs that any portion passing to a person under eighteen be retained and administered by the Trustee until majority. The two provisions give different answers for the same fund.

The incorporation of the statutory trust powers excludes "Subparagraphs 1 through _ inclusive", but the end of the excluded range is left blank or illegible, so the powers actually conferred cannot be determined from the instrument. Which statutory powers the Trustee holds is therefore genuinely open.

The successor-trustee article states only the triggering event (resignation or disqualification of the named bank) and then stops — "then the" — without naming a successor or a mechanism for appointing one. As it stands the clause supplies no operative direction.

The direction that the trust be governed "in all respects" by Tennessee law conflicts with the New York construction clause in the Metropolitan absolute assignment, a document expressly incorporated into this instrument by Article II. A court would have to decide which law governs the assigned ownership rights.

The exculpation excuses the Trustee "for any cause whatever except its own bad faith or negligence", so a clause that appears to be a broad immunity in fact preserves liability for ordinary negligence — the very standard it seems designed to disclaim. The reach of the exception is the point a court would have to fix.

The negligence carve-out cannot be squared with Article V, which says the Trustee "shall incur no liability" for purchases from or loans to the Grantor's estate, or with Article IV's "no obligation or duty whatever". The instrument states two different liability standards.

Irrevocability and the Grantor's relinquishment of all right to alter or amend sit uneasily with Article I.B, which reserves to the Grantor a continuing right to add property to the trust, and with Article II's power to surrender or cancel the Policies. Whether the trust is truly beyond the Grantor's reach is a question the instrument answers in two voices.

The assignment transfers "all right, title, interest, control, and incidents of ownership" and then lists specific rights "including specifically but not by way of limitation upon the generality of the foregoing", leaving the relation of the enumerated rights to the general grant to be worked out. Whether anything (for example the right to name a beneficiary contrary to the trust) falls outside the transfer is not settled by the text.

A New York construction clause in a document incorporated verbatim into the Trust Agreement contradicts Article XI, which provides that the trust shall in all respects be governed by Tennessee law. The two governing-law directions cannot both apply to the assigned policy rights.

The designation is garbled where it matters most: it "revocably designates" the Trustee (or the Group Policy and Certificate "itself as such Trustee") as beneficiary, so both the identity of the beneficiary and whether the designation is revocable or irrevocable are unclear. That uncertainty bears directly on who receives the proceeds.

A revocable beneficiary designation is hard to reconcile with Article XIII's declaration that the trust is irrevocable and with the absolute, gift-based assignment of ownership to the Trustee. The instrument thus points both ways on the permanence of the trust's entitlement to the proceeds.

The recital of the assignment leaves the assignor's name blank ("the irrevocable assignment by ___ to me") and the execution date open, so the consent identifies the transaction only by inference. That is a mechanical gap in a document that governs who the insurer must deal with.

"Eastman will look to no one else other than me" for contributory payments is immediately qualified by an exception permitting wage withholding from the employee and by Eastman's right to "recommence billing the assignee", so who is ultimately answerable for premiums shifts within one sentence. Whether the Trustee or the insured bears the risk of non-payment is arguable.

Reserving to Eastman and Metropolitan the right to amend or terminate the Policies is in tension with Article II of the trust, which vests the Trustee with "all rights of absolute ownership" and directs the insurer to recognise it as absolute owner. Whether the Trustee's ownership can be defeated by the policyholder's unilateral action is left unresolved between the two documents.
